summary: This work develops scalable lattice-surgery protocols for trivalent (degree-3) planar surface-code architectures and benchmarks them against conventional four-valent implementations. Trivalent lattice surgery eliminates the need for additional merging data qubits, reducing resource overhead by $\mathcal{O}(d)$ qubits and $\mathcal{O}(d)$ two-qubit gates while achieving up to ~25% logical-fidelity improvement at distance-3 in fluxonium-targeted simulations.
motivation: Reducing qubit connectivity from four to three neighbors aligns with hardware constraints of superconducting platforms, particularly fluxonium architectures where capacitive coupling limits make degree-4 connectivity challenging; simultaneously, understanding how lower valency affects both quantum-error-correction cycles and logical entanglement operations is essential for scalable fault-tolerant quantum processors.
method: Circuit constructions and numerically realistic simulations under standard circuit-level and experimentally motivated noise models targeting superconducting transmon parameters ($T_1 = 68$ µs, $T_2 = 89$ µs, two-qubit gate error 0.4%, gate time 47 ns) from Ref. [1], with decoder-based benchmarking of memory experiments and logical state teleportation via lattice surgery for distances $d = 3, 5, 7$.
result: Under standard noise, trivalent lattice surgery shows ~2% improvement at $d=3$ with reduced gate count ($2d^2$ gates versus $6d^2-2$); however, experimentally motivated noise including idling effects slightly disadvantages trivalent QEC cycles, though this can be compensated by reduced gate times ($\eta = 0.75$ achieves ~25% improvement for appropriate decoherence-dominated error models), particularly relevant for fluxonium where lower connectivity enables faster two-qubit gates via improved capacitive coupling.
